subject: Chemistry
title: One Atom, Many Lives: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
summary: In 1847 James Simpson found that chloroform, CHCl₃, could put people to sleep for surgery. Replace a hydrogen of a hydrocarbon with a halogen and you get a haloalkane (halogen on an sp³ alkyl carbon) or a haloarene (halogen on an sp² ring carbon). They are everywhere: chloramphenicol for typhoid, thyroxine with four iodine atoms, chloroquine for malaria, halothane for anaesthesia. The polar C–X bond, with a δ+ carbon, is why they react, and it opens the whole chapter.
keyPoints: **Definition**: replace an H of a hydrocarbon by a halogen X: a **haloalkane** (X on an sp³ alkyl carbon) or a **haloarene** (X on an sp² ring carbon).
**Chloroform (CHCl₃)**: methane with three H replaced by Cl; Simpson's anaesthetic, Edinburgh 1847.
**In medicine and the body**: chloramphenicol (typhoid), thyroxine (4 iodine; lack of iodine → goitre), chloroquine (malaria), halothane CF₃CHClBr (anaesthetic).
**Polar C–X bond**: X is more electronegative, so carbon is δ+ and is attacked by nucleophiles.
**Bond strength** falls C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I, so C–I breaks most easily.
**The other side**: freons deplete the ozone layer; DDT builds up along food chains.

quiz.explain: Cl is more electronegative, so C is δ+.
C–I is the longest and weakest C–X bond.
